importance_ranking.reason: Visual variation across built types is extreme — a 10×10 security guard cabin, a 40×10 bunkhouse, and a furnished site office are visually unrecognisable as the same product category. Buyers use the image to identify the correct sub-type before reading any text; wrong visual type causes an immediate skip.

Size (L×W) and Built Type are non-interchangeable — a contractor needing a 20×10 site office cannot substitute a 10×10 security cabin. These specs are the primary shortlisting gate; a listing without them cannot be evaluated or compared.

Price varies substantially with size and built type (plain shell vs furnished office vs bunkhouse), and the market is highly fragmented with hundreds of fabricators. Indian construction contractors actively compare prices across listings once size and type match; listed price is a real shortlisting signal.

importance_ranking.unit_note: Per piece is dominant for standard sizes (10×10, 10×15, 10×20 ft). Per sq ft is used for large custom or multi-room configurations — buyers comparing a per-piece quote against a per-sq-ft quote will misread price without unit clarity.
importance_ranking.reason: Unit must be shown because the market has two active quoting conventions (per piece and per sq ft) and a buyer comparing standard-size listings against custom-configuration listings will misread price if unit is absent.

importance_ranking.brand_important_reason: No dominant brand with buyer recall exists in this category — taxonomy siblings contain no branded MS cabin MCATs and the market is fragmented across hundreds of regional fabricators.
importance_ranking.reason: Seller capability — fabrication quality, installation service, delivery radius, and track record on similar projects — matters to institutional and government buyers during vendor selection, but company ranks last as buyers shortlist on image, specs, and price first.

top_configurator_specs.reason: Defines what the cabin IS and who it is for — a bunkhouse, site office, security cabin, and toilet block are non-interchangeable products targeting different buyer segments with substantially different price points.

Floor area is the primary price driver — price scales directly with size, and a buyer needing 20×10 ft cannot substitute 10×10 ft, making this a non-interchangeable configurator with the largest absolute price delta in the spec list.

missing_important_specs.why_important: Frame section size (e.g., 100×50mm C-channel vs 50×50mm square pipe) is a primary structural quality differentiator that institutional and government buyers use to compare durability and justify price differences between fabricators.

Whether the cabin is supplied as a knock-down kit, a ready-to-install unit, or with full installation service materially changes the buyer's logistics cost and total project cost, and sellers need this to quote accurately.

GI/MS sheet gauge (e.g., 0.5mm vs 0.8mm) directly affects structural durability and weather resistance, and is a standard comparison point for buyers evaluating quality across fabricators in this fragmented market.

top_rfq_specs.reason: Application defines the use case and built type — a seller specialising in security cabins or sanitation blocks may not supply furnished site offices, so this spec routes the RFQ to sellers who can actually fulfil the requirement.

Length is the primary size dimension that determines whether a seller can fabricate or supply the required cabin and allows accurate price quotation — sellers cannot respond meaningfully without knowing the required footprint.

missing_important_specs.why_important: Sellers need to know whether the buyer wants a plain shell, a furnished unit, or a cabin with electrical fittings and AC provision — this determines the scope of supply and drives the largest price variation within the same size and application.
